paragraphs.heading: The ingredient that runs out
paragraphs.text: In a chemical reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant that is completely used up by the time the reaction finishes. Once it is gone the reaction cannot go on, so it sets a ceiling on how much product forms. Any other reactants left over, because more was present than the limiting reagent could react with, are called excess reagents, sometimes shortened to "xs".

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: You need to know the limiting reagent before you can work out a reaction's percentage yield. That is because the theoretical yield is defined as the product you would get if the limiting reagent reacted completely. Starting from the balanced chemical equation, there are several equivalent ways to find the limiting reagent and to work out how much of each other reactant is left in excess.

paragraphs.heading: Method one: compare what is needed
paragraphs.text: Choose one reactant, call it A, and use the balanced equation to work out how much of the other reactant, B, it would need. If more B is actually present than that, B is the excess reagent and A limits the reaction. If less B is present, B is the limiting reagent. This approach works best when there are just two reactants.

paragraphs.heading: A worked case with benzene
paragraphs.text: Take a reaction of benzene with oxygen. With 18 mol of O₂ on hand, 18 − 11.25 = 6.75 mol of oxygen is still unreacted once every bit of benzene is consumed. Oxygen is therefore the reagent in excess, and benzene is the limiting reagent.

paragraphs.heading: Method two: compare the product
paragraphs.text: A second approach uses the equation to work out how much of one product each reactant could make from the amount present. Whichever reactant would make the least product is the limiting one. Unlike the first method, it extends easily to three, four or more reactants. In one example, the amounts of Al and Fe₂O₃ are given in grams, so both are first turned into moles. The Al present could yield 0.297 mol of Fe but the Fe₂O₃ only 0.250 mol, so the Fe₂O₃ limits how much Fe forms.

paragraphs.heading: Method three: extent of reaction
paragraphs.text: A third way works out, for each reagent, the extent of reaction needed to bring it down to zero. The reagent that runs out at the lowest extent is the limiting reagent. Multiplying that extent by each other chemical's stoichiometric coefficient then gives how much of each chemical there is when the reaction ends.
